# The Value of Disagreement: Why the Best Meetings Don't End in Consensus

## Rethinking What a Successful Meeting Looks Like

There is a common assumption, woven deep into workplace culture, that a good meeting is one where everyone walks out nodding. We celebrate alignment. We praise teams for being "on the same page." A meeting that ends in consensus feels productive; a meeting that ends in argument feels like a failure, or at least an unfinished piece of business.

But this assumption deserves scrutiny. Agreement, it turns out, can be deceptive. People nod along for many reasons that have nothing to do with genuine conviction: fatigue, deference to the most senior person in the room, the desire to end a meeting that has already run twenty minutes long, or simple reluctance to be the lone dissenting voice. When a meeting ends with everyone agreeing, we may have achieved harmony—or we may have merely buried our disagreements where no one can see them. And buried disagreements have a way of resurfacing later, usually at the worst possible moment, when the cost of being wrong has grown.
